Figure 7 shows how natural-language instructions steer compaction timing, semantic boundaries, and backup behavior. The figure consists of three panels.

The first panel shows the timing of the first compaction. For the no-instruction control, the first compaction occurs at 16k tokens. When instructed to compact once the context reaches a specific threshold, the agent follows the instruction closely: for a 16k threshold, the median is 16.0k tokens; for 24k, it is 23.6k tokens; and for 32k, it is 30.9k tokens.

The second panel shows compaction around sub-question boundaries. Without instruction, the rate of compaction within two turns of a boundary is 0.2. With the instruction to compact at sub-question boundaries, this rate increases to 0.6.

The third panel shows backup behavior. Without instruction, no edits are preceded by a backup. With the instruction to back up on disk before compacting, 68 percent of edits are preceded by a full backup, and 88 percent are preceded by either a full or partial backup.
</NARRATION>
<SUMMARY>
Figure 7 demonstrates that natural-language instructions can steer a CLM's context-management policy. It shows the agent accurately follows instructions regarding compaction thresholds, semantic boundaries, and backup behavior.
</SUMMARY>
<TAGS>
context management, prompt steering, compaction, backup behavior
</TAGS>

Figure 7 shows how a single sentence in the prompt changes the context-management policy, steering compaction timing, semantic boundaries, and backup behavior. Gray denotes no instruction and blue the instructed setting.

The figure consists of three panels. The first panel shows the effect of the instruction, "Compact to 4k tokens once you reach Y tokens." It plots the instructed threshold Y on the x-axis against the context size at first compaction on the y-axis. For the no-instruction control, the first compaction occurs at a constant 38,000 tokens. In contrast, the instructed agent follows the threshold closely: at a 16k threshold, first compaction occurs at 16.0k tokens; at 24k, it occurs at 23.6k tokens; and at 32k, it occurs at 30.9k tokens.

The second panel shows the effect of the instruction, "Compact at sub-question boundaries." It plots the number of turns after a sub-question boundary on the x-axis against the rate of boundaries compacted at that turn on the y-axis. Without instruction, the rate is 0.34 at the boundary and 0.40 within two turns. With the instruction, the rate peaks sharply at 0.77 at the boundary, and 0.88 of boundaries are compacted within two turns.

The third panel shows the effect of the instruction, "Back up on disk before you compact." It compares the fraction of edits preceded by a backup between the no-instruction and instructed settings. Without instruction, the fraction is 0.00. With the instruction, 0.68 of edits are preceded by a full backup and 0.80 are preceded by either a full or partial backup, an increase of 0.09 over the full backup rate.
</NARRATION>
<SUMMARY>
Figure 7 demonstrates that natural-language instructions can steer a CLM's context-management policy. It shows the agent successfully adapting its compaction timing, boundary detection, and backup behavior based on prompt instructions.
</SUMMARY>

context management, prompt steering, compaction policy

Figure 9 compares Suffix Cache Reuse and standard SGLang serving on BCP with Qwen3.6-27B. The left panel shows that Suffix Cache Reuse achieves a task accuracy of 73.9 percent, slightly higher than the 72.9 percent of standard SGLang, while reducing the prefix-reuse FLOPs per question from 10.98 to 7.14. The right panel decomposes server-side compute by the fraction of prompt tokens. Across all turns, standard SGLang has 27.1 percent of tokens as prefix-cache hits, while Suffix Cache Reuse has 73.9 percent as hits, 7.8 percent as reused by Suffix Cache Reuse, and 18.3 percent as prefilled. For turns following context edits, standard SGLang has 75.8 percent of tokens prefilled and 24.2 percent as hits; in contrast, Suffix Cache Reuse has 29.9 percent as hits, 28.2 percent as reused by Suffix Cache Reuse, and 41.8 percent as prefilled.
</NARRATION>
<SUMMARY>
Figure 9 compares Suffix Cache Reuse and standard SGLang on BCP using Qwen3.6-27B. It shows Suffix Cache Reuse improves accuracy and reduces FLOPs, while significantly increasing the fraction of cache hits and reused tokens across all turns and edited turns.
</SUMMARY>

Figure 11 shows a small-scale sensitivity study of relocated spans per edit, K, using 64 BrowseComp-Plus questions with Qwen3.6-27B. The figure consists of three plots. The middle plot shows prefix-reuse PFLOPs per question, where the cost decreases as K increases, with the gains largely saturating by K equals 6. The right plot shows relocated tokens per edited request, which increases as K increases. In all three plots, the column for K equals 6 is shaded to indicate it is the value used elsewhere in the work. Dashed lines represent standard SGLang, and hollow markers represent a repeat run. Error bars indicate plus or minus one standard error across questions, and a gray band indicates plus or minus one standard error for standard SGLang.
</NARRATION>
<SUMMARY>
Figure 11 presents a sensitivity analysis of the parameter K on accuracy, PFLOPs, and relocated tokens. It shows that accuracy is robust and cache-reuse gains saturate around K=6.
</SUMMARY>

Table 4 compares excerpts of the KV Store skill for each method. Every skill provides guidance on four points: how the mechanism works, what to do with each batch, how to answer a query, and how to confirm that a step worked.

For CLM, the mechanism mirrors context to an editable file. For each batch, the model uses a python3 heredoc command to move the block to a temporary directory on disk. To handle a GET, it uses grep to recover the value from that directory. A failure is confirmed if there is no note or if the token count does not drop.

For ACM, the manage_context tool replaces history with a summary message. For each batch, the model monitors a gauge and calls manage_context when it exceeds 22,000 tokens. To handle a GET, it spends one turn calling query_memory for the specific summary covering the key. Success is confirmed by the summary message and a lower token readout.

For RLM, the mechanism relies on the persistence of the REPL namespace. For each batch, the model defines a store and handler once, then calls them using a dictionary filled by a regular expression. A GET is answered by placing the answer block in the content of the answer variable. Success is confirmed by printing the output to show the number of stored keys growing by one per SET operation.

For Context Folding, a branch is created from a copy of the context, meaning the main context remains full. For each batch, the model runs only the echo READY_FOR_NEXT_OP command in the main context. To handle a GET, it finds the SET line in the batch currently in front of it. Success is confirmed if the token readout rises only by the size of each batch.

For Self-Compact, compression occurs when specific conditions for C and N are met, replacing history with a summary. For each batch, the model copies the block to its own file and answers the probe to trigger compression. To handle a GET, it uses grep to find the value in the store files. Success is confirmed when grep returns a count of 100.

For Summary, the mechanism replaces everything except the system prompt and task message with one message once three quarters of the budget is reached, which is about 24.6K of 32,768 tokens. For each batch, the model copies the block to its own file and writes the summary as a pointer. To handle a GET, it uses grep to find the value in the store files. Success is confirmed when grep returns a count of 100.

For the Base method, every operation stays in the context for the rest of the run with no way to remove it. For each batch, the model runs one command and does not copy batches to disk. To handle a GET, it finds the SET line in the batch already sitting in its context. Success is confirmed if the token readout rises by the size of each batch and almost nothing else.
